text:
## Theoretical Part

First, some math... The derivations below are somewhat complex, so do not worry if you don't follow everything. Luckily, the final loss function is simple and intuitive. The derivation is not necessary to understand the code, but gives a very nice interpretation of the final loss function.

This follows a nice derivation of Contrastive Divergence found in https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~ojw/files/NotesOnCD.pdf. If you reference the above, keep in mind a change of notation: our $E$ is the same as $-log(f)$ in the derivation (equivalently $f = e^{-E}$).

We will derive the loss function for our energy based models using maximum likelihood. Later we will see that the resulting loss function makes sense even if we don't transform the energy into a probability distribution.

Start with an energy defined for all inputs $x$ and dependent on parameters $w$: $E(x, w)$. We use regular letters $x$ and $w$, but keep in mind that they represent vectors (many parameters and many input variables for each input). In addition, for many derivations and analytical results it is convenient to think of $x$ as being a continuous scalar variable instead of a high-dimensional vector. It should be clear from the context, i.e. if we integrate over $x$ it is a continuous variable, if we sum over values $x_i$ of $x$, it is a discrete vector.

Note: in the practical part below, $x$ will be a tensor of image pixels and $w$ the weights in the neural network, in other words the neural network calculates the energy and we will see that we want to train it (tune the parameters $w$), so that it gives low energy to realistic images and high energy to fake images.

We can transform $E$ into a probability by normalizing it as follows:

$p(x,w) = \dfrac{1}{Z(w)} e^{-E(x,w)}$,

where

$Z(w) = \int e^{-E(x,w)}$.

Here we are assuming that $x$ is a continuous variable, so the integration is analogous to summation in the case of $x$ being discrete valued. If you are not familiar with integration, just think about it being aproximated by "summing" the energy values over the possible values of $x$ (all possible images in our example). This should actually look familiar. Remember the softmax activation? In the discrete case, this is how we usually turn multiple outputs into a probability distribution used for classification in a neural network.

The difference is that we are only using this form now to derive an appropriate loss function - with energy models, our loss function will work directly with unnormalized energy values.

Now that we have a probability function, we can use the usual Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

$loss = -\mathbb{E}_{x \sim data} \log p(x,w) = -\dfrac{1}{N} \sum \log p(x_i, w) = -\dfrac{1}{N} \sum \log \left( \dfrac{1}{Z(w)} e^{-E(x_i,w)} \right) = \dfrac{1}{N} \sum \left( \log Z(w) -E(x_i, w) \right)$.

Since $Z$ doesn't depend on $i$ or $x$ this simplifies to

$loss = \log Z(w) + \dfrac{1}{N} \sum E(x_i, w)$.

To train a neural network using gradient descent requires calculating the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters $w$:

$\nabla_w loss = \nabla_w \log Z(w) + \dfrac{1}{N} \sum \nabla_w E(x_i, w) = \nabla_w \log Z(w) + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim data} \nabla_w E(x, w)$.

We will obtain a form for the first term in terms of an expectation as well.

$\nabla_w \log Z(w) = \dfrac{1}{Z(w)} \nabla_w Z(w) = \dfrac{1}{Z(w)} \nabla_w \int e^{-E(x,w)} dx = -\dfrac{1}{Z(w)} \int e^{- E(x,w)} \nabla_w E(x,w) dx = -\dfrac{1}{Z(w)} \int e^{- E(x,w)} \nabla_w E(x,w) dx = -\int p(x,w) \nabla_w E(x,w) dx = - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim model} \nabla_w E(x,w)$

and the full gradient becomes

$\nabla_w loss = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim data} \nabla_w E(x, w) - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim model} \nabla_w E(x,w)$.

In other words, minimizing this loss is equivalent to finding parameters $w$ that decrease the energy on the data and increase the energy on the model. This is a form of contrastive divergence, where we are trying to minimize the difference between the data and the model distributions. It penalizes $x$ values "away" from the data distribution.

text:
We now construct the neural network that approximates the energy $E(x,w)$. The architecture is a familiar convolutional neural network, with a small addition of using the `swish` activation function instead of ReLU that we've been using before. The convolutional layers reduce the image from 32 by 32 to 2 by 2 and increase the number of channels from 1 to 64. The final fully connected layers reduce the output to a single scalar value representing the energy of the input image.

```python
# Swish activation function
def swish(x):
    return x * torch.sigmoid(x)

class EnergyModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(EnergyModel, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 16, kernel_size=5, stride=2, padding=2)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(16, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)
        self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(32, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)
        self.conv4 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1)

        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(64 * 2 * 2, 64)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(64, 1)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = swish(self.conv1(x))
        x = swish(self.conv2(x))
        x = swish(self.conv3(x))
        x = swish(self.conv4(x))
        x = self.flatten(x)
        x = swish(self.fc1(x))
        return self.fc2(x)
```

text:
We next create a function that samples the low energy states. We assume that we have a neural network represented by `nn_model` that maps input images to energy (often you will see the neural network designed to model negative energy $-E$ instead of $E$ as a convention, in which case you should be careful with either switching the sign before doing gradient descent or doing gradient ascent instead by adding a multiple of the gradient instead of subtracting it.)

```python
def generate_samples(nn_energy_model, inp_imgs, steps, step_size, noise_std):
    nn_energy_model.eval()

    # As we do various calculations on the input images (like adding noise)
    # these are added to the computational graph, however we really only
    # need this for computing gradients during backpropogation.

    # Energy: (x, w) => E(x, w)
    # For sampling we fix the weights, and perform gradient descent with derivatives with respect to x
    # for w in nn_energy_model.parameters():
    #     w.requires_grad = False
    # inp_imgs = inp_imgs.detach().requires_grad_(True)

    for _ in range(steps):
        # We add noise to the input images, but we will
        # need to calculate the gradients with the transformed
        # noisy images, so tell pytorch not to track the gradient 
        # yet, this way we can avoid unnecessary computations that
        # pytorch does in order to calculate the gradients later:
        with torch.no_grad():
            noise = torch.randn_like(inp_imgs) * noise_std
            inp_imgs = (inp_imgs + noise).clamp(-1.0, 1.0)

        inp_imgs.requires_grad_(True)

        # Compute energy and gradients
        energy = nn_energy_model(inp_imgs)

        # The gradient with respect to parameters is usually done automatically 
        # when we train a neural network as part of .backward() call.
        # Here we do it manually and specify that the gradient should be with 
        # respect to the input images, not the parameters.
        # In addition because energy contains energy values for each input image
        # in a batch, we need to specify an extra grad_outputs argument for the 
        # right gradients to be calculated for each input image.
        grads, = torch.autograd.grad(energy, inp_imgs, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(energy))

        # Finally, apply gradient clipping for stabilizing the sampling
        with torch.no_grad():
            grads = grads.clamp(-0.03, 0.03)
            inp_imgs = (inp_imgs - step_size*grads).clamp(-1.0, 1.0)

    return inp_imgs.detach()

# We can also use .backward() call to calculate the gradient instead of autograd.grad
# The difference is that pytorch will automatically populate the gradients into
# .grad attribute of the input tensor instead of returning it.
```

text:
The `generate_samples` function above uses a process called *Langevin Dynamics* to generate points based on the energy defined by our neural network model. It turned out that this works only after an initial amount of gradient steps referred to as mixing time. This makes generating samples from scratch every time inefficient. One way to address this is to keep a buffer of samples and sample from it instead of starting from random noise every time. This is implemented in the `Buffer` class below.

```python
class Buffer:
    def __init__(self, model, device):
        super().__init__()
        self.model = model
        self.device = device
        # start with random images in the buffer
        self.examples = [torch.rand((1, 1, 32, 32), device=self.device) * 2 - 1 for _ in range(128)]

    def sample_new_exmps(self, steps, step_size, noise):
        n_new = np.random.binomial(128, 0.05)

        # Generate new random images for around 5% of the inputs
        new_rand_imgs = torch.rand((n_new, 1, 32, 32),  device=self.device) * 2 - 1

        # Sample old images from the buffer for the rest
        old_imgs = torch.cat(random.choices(self.examples, k=128 - n_new), dim=0)

        inp_imgs = torch.cat([new_rand_imgs, old_imgs], dim=0)

        # Run Langevin dynamics
        new_imgs = generate_samples(self.model, inp_imgs, steps, step_size, noise)

        # Update buffer
        self.examples = list(torch.split(new_imgs, 1, dim=0)) + self.examples
        self.examples = self.examples[:8192]

        return new_imgs
```

text:
Finally define, the Energy class which will be responsible for tuning the weights of our energy model in order to increase the energy on the generated images and decrease it on the training data images.

```python
from collections import defaultdict

class Metric:
    def __init__(self):
        self.reset()

    def update(self, val):
        self.total += val.item()
        self.count += 1

    def result(self):
        return self.total / self.count if self.count > 0 else 0.0

    def reset(self):
        self.total = 0.0
        self.count = 0

class EBM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model, alpha, steps, step_size, noise, device):
        super().__init__()
        self.device = device
        # define the nn energy model 
        self.model = model

        self.buffer = Buffer(self.model, device=device)

        # define the hyperparameters
        self.alpha = alpha
        self.steps = steps
        self.step_size = step_size
        self.noise = noise

        self.loss_metric = Metric()
        self.reg_loss_metric = Metric()
        self.cdiv_loss_metric = Metric()
        self.real_out_metric = Metric()
        self.fake_out_metric = Metric()

    def metrics(self):
        return {
            "loss": self.loss_metric.result(),
            "reg": self.reg_loss_metric.result(),
            "cdiv": self.cdiv_loss_metric.result(),
            "real": self.real_out_metric.result(),
            "fake": self.fake_out_metric.result()
        }

    def reset_metrics(self):
        for m in [self.loss_metric, self.reg_loss_metric, self.cdiv_loss_metric,
                  self.real_out_metric, self.fake_out_metric]:
            m.reset()

    def train_step(self, real_imgs, optimizer):
        real_imgs = real_imgs + torch.randn_like(real_imgs) * self.noise
        real_imgs = torch.clamp(real_imgs, -1.0, 1.0)


        fake_imgs = self.buffer.sample_new_exmps(
            steps=self.steps, step_size=self.step_size, noise=self.noise)

        inp_imgs = torch.cat([real_imgs, fake_imgs], dim=0)
        inp_imgs = inp_imgs.clone().detach().to(device).requires_grad_(False)

        out_scores = self.model(inp_imgs)

        real_out, fake_out = torch.split(out_scores, [real_imgs.size(0), fake_imgs.size(0)], dim=0)

        cdiv_loss = real_out.mean() - fake_out.mean() 
        reg_loss = self.alpha * (real_out.pow(2).mean() + fake_out.pow(2).mean())
        loss = cdiv_loss + reg_loss 

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()

        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(self.model.parameters(), max_norm=0.1)

        optimizer.step()

        self.loss_metric.update(loss)
        self.reg_loss_metric.update(reg_loss)
        self.cdiv_loss_metric.update(cdiv_loss)
        self.real_out_metric.update(real_out.mean())
        self.fake_out_metric.update(fake_out.mean())

        return self.metrics()

    def test_step(self, real_imgs):
        batch_size = real_imgs.shape[0]
        fake_imgs = torch.rand((batch_size, 1, 32, 32), device=self.device) * 2 - 1
        inp_imgs = torch.cat([real_imgs, fake_imgs], dim=0)

        with torch.no_grad():
            out_scores = self.model(inp_imgs)
            real_out, fake_out = torch.split(out_scores, batch_size, dim=0)
            cdiv = real_out.mean() - fake_out.mean()

        self.cdiv_loss_metric.update(cdiv)
        self.real_out_metric.update(real_out.mean())
        self.fake_out_metric.update(fake_out.mean())

        return {
            "cdiv": self.cdiv_loss_metric.result(),
            "real": self.real_out_metric.result(),
            "fake": self.fake_out_metric.result()
        }
```

text:
### Training the energy based model

Each epoch alternates between pushing the energy *down* on real MNIST digits and *up* on the
samples drawn from the replay buffer by Langevin dynamics (contrastive divergence).

Note this is slow: every training batch runs `steps=60` Langevin updates through the network.
Lower `EPOCHS` (or `steps`) if you just want to see it working.

```python
EPOCHS = 10

# Initialize model, EBM wrapper and optimizer
nn_energy_model = EnergyModel().to(device)
ebm = EBM(nn_energy_model, alpha=0.1, steps=60, step_size=10, noise=0.005, device=device)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(nn_energy_model.parameters(), lr=0.0001, betas=(0.0, 0.999))

# Training loop
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    ebm.reset_metrics()
    metrics = {}
    for batch in train_loader:
        real_imgs = batch[0].to(device, non_blocking=PIN_MEMORY)
        metrics = ebm.train_step(real_imgs, optimizer)

    # The buffer *prepends* freshly sampled images, so examples[:8] are the newest
    # ones (examples[-8:] would show the stalest entries in the replay buffer).
    plot_samples(torch.cat(ebm.buffer.examples[:8]), n=8)
    print(f"Epoch {epoch+1} - " + ", ".join(f"{k}: {v:.4f}" for k, v in metrics.items()))

    # Validation step
    ebm.reset_metrics()
    val_metrics = {}
    for batch in test_loader:
        real_imgs = batch[0].to(device, non_blocking=PIN_MEMORY)
        val_metrics = ebm.test_step(real_imgs)

    print("Validation - " + ", ".join(f"{k}: {v:.4f}" for k, v in val_metrics.items()))
```

text:
# Module 7: Practical 2 - Diffusion Methods

Recall that the idea behind Diffusion Models is to map training data to a simple normal distribution by adding noise through a series of steps and then have a neural network **learn** the inverse process.

In contrast to autoencoders, the first step is done through simple well defined functions and only the decoder is learned.

text:
Let's take $x_0$ to be a random variable representing images in our data distribution. We will assume that it has mean $0$ and variance $1$. This is ok since we have preprocessed the training images to have mean $0$ and variance $1$.

Next, we will corrupt the images by adding standard gaussian noise $\epsilon$ (mean 0, variance 1). How much noise should be added?

To keep the transformed distribution having the same mean and variance, we can control the noise amount using a parameter $\beta$:

$x_1 = \sqrt{1-\beta}x_0 + \sqrt{\beta} \epsilon$

Then if $x_0$ has mean $0$ and variance $1$, $x_1$ will have mean:

$\sqrt{1-\beta}*0+\sqrt{\beta}*0=0$

and variance:

$(\sqrt{1-\beta})^2*1 + (\sqrt{\beta})^2*1=1-\beta+\beta=1$.

```python
def corrupt_image(image, beta=0.1):
    # Stay in torch (mixing in np.random.normal would silently upcast to float64).
    noise = torch.randn_like(image)
    image_with_noise = math.sqrt(1 - beta) * image + math.sqrt(beta) * noise
    return image_with_noise
```

text:
We can repeat this process using the new $x_1$ as the input to the next step, and so on, until we reach $x_T$. Moreover, we can also use a different $\beta$ for each step. The setup of how this parameter should vary is referred to as the **diffusion schedule**.

We'll want to repeat this process through several iterations, at each step corrupting the image by a small amount. To make things simpler, we can perform some mathematical magic using the fact that multiplying a Gaussian distribution by a constant results in another Gaussian distribution. Similarly, adding two Gaussians results in a Gaussian. So, one can show mathematically that for two standard Gaussian random variables:

$A \epsilon_0 + B \epsilon_1 = \left(\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}\right)\epsilon$, where $\epsilon$ is also a Gaussian random variable.

Hence,

$x_2 = \sqrt{1-\beta_1}x_1 + \sqrt{\beta_1} \epsilon_1 = \sqrt{1-\beta_1}(\sqrt{1-\beta_0}x_0 + \sqrt{\beta_0} \epsilon_0) + \sqrt{\beta_1} \epsilon_1 = \sqrt{(1-\beta_0)(1-\beta_1)}x_0 + \sqrt{\beta_0(1-\beta_1)}\epsilon_0 + \sqrt{\beta_1}\epsilon_1 = \sqrt{(1-\beta_0)(1-\beta_1)}x_0 + \sqrt{1 - (1-\beta_0)(1-\beta_1)}\epsilon$,

and so on. This will be used in defining the multipliers for the image (signal rates) and the noise (noise rates).

Let's look at examples of several diffusion schedules:

The idea is to train a neural network to model the noise that was added. The input to this network will be the noisy image and the variance of the noise that was added (this comes from the diffusion schedule we select). The noise variance is typically encoded using some sort of an embedding, in this case a Sinusoidal Embedding.

```python
import math

class SinusoidalEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_frequencies=16):
        super().__init__()
        self.num_frequencies = num_frequencies
        frequencies = torch.exp(torch.linspace(math.log(1.0), math.log(1000.0), num_frequencies))
        self.register_buffer("angular_speeds", 2.0 * math.pi * frequencies.view(1, 1, 1, -1))

    def forward(self, x):
        """
        x: Tensor of shape (B, 1, 1, 1)
        returns: Tensor of shape (B, 1, 1, 2 * num_frequencies)
        """
        x = x.expand(-1, 1, 1, self.num_frequencies)
        sin_part = torch.sin(self.angular_speeds * x)
        cos_part = torch.cos(self.angular_speeds * x)
        return torch.cat([sin_part, cos_part], dim=-1)
```

```python
def linear_diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times, min_rate=1e-4, max_rate=0.02, num_steps=1000):
    """
    diffusion_times: Tensor of any shape, with values in [0, 1)
    Returns:
        noise_rates, signal_rates: Tensors with the SAME shape as diffusion_times

    Note: alpha_bar is the cumulative product *along the diffusion schedule*. We therefore
    build the schedule once on a fixed grid of `num_steps` and then look up each sample's
    time on it. (Running `cumprod` directly on `diffusion_times` would multiply across the
    batch dimension, making each sample's noise level depend on the other samples.)
    """
    diffusion_times = diffusion_times.to(dtype=torch.float32)

    betas = torch.linspace(min_rate, max_rate, num_steps, device=diffusion_times.device)
    alpha_bars = torch.cumprod(1.0 - betas, dim=0)

    idx = (diffusion_times * (num_steps - 1)).long().clamp(0, num_steps - 1)
    alpha_bars_t = alpha_bars[idx]

    signal_rates = torch.sqrt(alpha_bars_t)
    noise_rates = torch.sqrt(1.0 - alpha_bars_t)
    return noise_rates, signal_rates


def cosine_diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times):
    # diffusion_times: Tensor of shape [T] or [B] with values in [0, 1]
    signal_rates = torch.cos(diffusion_times * math.pi / 2)
    noise_rates = torch.sin(diffusion_times * math.pi / 2)
    return noise_rates, signal_rates


def offset_cosine_diffusion_schedule(diffusion_times, min_signal_rate=0.02, max_signal_rate=0.95):
    # Flatten diffusion_times to handle any shape
    original_shape = diffusion_times.shape
    diffusion_times_flat = diffusion_times.flatten()

    # Compute start and end angles from signal rate bounds
    start_angle = torch.acos(torch.tensor(max_signal_rate, dtype=torch.float32, device=diffusion_times.device))
    end_angle = torch.acos(torch.tensor(min_signal_rate, dtype=torch.float32, device=diffusion_times.device))

    # Linearly interpolate angles
    diffusion_angles = start_angle + diffusion_times_flat * (end_angle - start_angle)

    # Compute signal and noise rates
    signal_rates = torch.cos(diffusion_angles).reshape(original_shape)
    noise_rates = torch.sin(diffusion_angles).reshape(original_shape)

    return noise_rates, signal_rates
```

Next we build the three new layers used in a UNet neural network, a popular architecture used in Diffusion Models.

```python
class ResidualBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.needs_projection = in_channels != out_channels
        if self.needs_projection:
            self.proj = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=1)
        else:
            self.proj = nn.Identity()

        self.norm = nn.BatchNorm2d(in_channels, affine=False)
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(in_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)
        self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(out_channels, out_channels, kernel_size=3, padding=1)

    def swish(self, x):
        return x * torch.sigmoid(x)

    def forward(self, x):
        residual = self.proj(x)
        # x = self.norm(x)
        x = self.swish(self.conv1(x))
        x = self.conv2(x)
        return x + residual

class DownBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width, block_depth, in_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        for i in range(block_depth):
            self.blocks.append(ResidualBlock(in_channels, width))
            in_channels = width
        self.pool = nn.AvgPool2d(kernel_size=2)

    def forward(self, x, skips):
        for block in self.blocks:
            x = block(x)
            skips.append(x)
        x = self.pool(x)
        return x

class UpBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, width, block_depth, in_channels):
        super().__init__()
        self.blocks = nn.ModuleList()
        for _ in range(block_depth):
            self.blocks.append(ResidualBlock(in_channels + width, width))
            in_channels = width

    def forward(self, x, skips):
        x = F.interpolate(x, scale_factor=2, mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)
        for block in self.blocks:
            skip = skips.pop()
            x = torch.cat([x, skip], dim=1)
            x = block(x)
        return x
```

```python
class UNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, image_size, num_channels, embedding_dim=32):
        super().__init__()
        self.initial = nn.Conv2d(num_channels, 32, kernel_size=1)
        self.num_channels = num_channels
        self.image_size = image_size
        self.embedding_dim = embedding_dim
        self.embedding = SinusoidalEmbedding(num_frequencies=16)
        self.embedding_proj = nn.Conv2d(embedding_dim, 32, kernel_size=1)

        self.down1 = DownBlock(32, in_channels=64, block_depth=2)
        self.down2 = DownBlock(64, in_channels=32, block_depth=2)
        self.down3 = DownBlock(96, in_channels=64, block_depth=2) 

        self.mid1 = ResidualBlock(in_channels=96, out_channels=128)
        self.mid2 = ResidualBlock(in_channels=128, out_channels=128)

        self.up1 = UpBlock(96, in_channels=128, block_depth=2) 
        self.up2 = UpBlock(64, block_depth=2, in_channels=96)
        self.up3 = UpBlock(32, block_depth=2, in_channels=64)

        self.final = nn.Conv2d(32, num_channels, kernel_size=1)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.final.weight)  # Keep zero init like TF reference

    def forward(self, noisy_images, noise_variances):
        skips = []
        x = self.initial(noisy_images)
        noise_emb = self.embedding(noise_variances)  # shape: (B, 1, 1, 32)
        # Upsample to match image size like TF reference
        noise_emb = F.interpolate(noise_emb.permute(0, 3, 1, 2), size=(self.image_size, self.image_size), mode='nearest')
        x = torch.cat([x, noise_emb], dim=1)

        x = self.down1(x, skips)
        x = self.down2(x, skips) 
        x = self.down3(x, skips)    

        x = self.mid1(x)     
        x = self.mid2(x)   

        x = self.up1(x, skips)
        x = self.up2(x, skips)
        x = self.up3(x, skips)

        return self.final(x)
```

```python
import copy

class DiffusionModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, model, schedule_fn):
        super().__init__()
        self.network = model
        self.ema_network = copy.deepcopy(model)
        self.ema_network.eval()
        self.ema_decay = 0.8
        self.schedule_fn = schedule_fn
        self.normalizer_mean = 0.0
        self.normalizer_std = 1.0

    def to(self, device):
        # Override to() to ensure both networks move to the same device
        super().to(device)
        self.ema_network.to(device)
        return self

    def set_normalizer(self, mean, std):
        self.normalizer_mean = mean
        self.normalizer_std = std

    def denormalize(self, x):
        return torch.clamp(x * self.normalizer_std + self.normalizer_mean, 0.0, 1.0)

    def denoise(self, noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates, training):
        # Use EMA network for inference, main network for training
        if training:
            network = self.network
            network.train()
        else:
            network = self.ema_network
            network.eval()

        pred_noises = network(noisy_images, noise_rates ** 2)
        pred_images = (noisy_images - noise_rates * pred_noises) / signal_rates
        return pred_noises, pred_images

    def reverse_diffusion(self, initial_noise, diffusion_steps):
        step_size = 1.0 / diffusion_steps
        current_images = initial_noise
        for step in range(diffusion_steps):
            t = torch.ones((initial_noise.shape[0], 1, 1, 1), device=initial_noise.device) * (1 - step * step_size)
            noise_rates, signal_rates = self.schedule_fn(t)
            pred_noises, pred_images = self.denoise(current_images, noise_rates, signal_rates, training=False)

            # Debug generation process
            if step % max(1, diffusion_steps // 4) == 0:  # Print 4 times during generation
                print(f"Generation Step {step}/{diffusion_steps}: t={1-step*step_size:.3f}")
                print(f"  Current images std: {current_images.std().item():.4f}")
                print(f"  Pred images std: {pred_images.std().item():.4f}")
                print(f"  Signal rate: {signal_rates.mean().item():.4f}, Noise rate: {noise_rates.mean().item():.4f}")

            next_diffusion_times = t - step_size
            next_noise_rates, next_signal_rates = self.schedule_fn(next_diffusion_times)
            current_images = next_signal_rates * pred_images + next_noise_rates * pred_noises
        return pred_images

    def generate(self, num_images, diffusion_steps, image_size=64, initial_noise=None):
        if initial_noise is None:
            initial_noise = torch.randn((num_images, self.network.num_channels, image_size, image_size), device=next(self.parameters()).device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            return self.denormalize(self.reverse_diffusion(initial_noise, diffusion_steps))

    def train_step(self, images, optimizer, loss_fn):
        images = (images - self.normalizer_mean) / self.normalizer_std
        noises = torch.randn_like(images)

        diffusion_times = torch.rand((images.size(0), 1, 1, 1), device=images.device)
        noise_rates, signal_rates = self.schedule_fn(diffusion_times)
        noisy_images = signal_rates * images + noise_rates * noises

        pred_noises, _ = self.denoise(noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates, training=True)
        loss = loss_fn(pred_noises, noises)

        # Debug prints
        if torch.rand(1).item() < 0.01:  # Print more frequently to see output
            print(f"Debug - Loss: {loss.item():.4f}, Noise std: {noises.std().item():.4f}, Pred std: {pred_noises.std().item():.4f}")
            print(f"Signal rates range: {signal_rates.min().item():.4f}-{signal_rates.max().item():.4f}")
            print(f"Noise rates range: {noise_rates.min().item():.4f}-{noise_rates.max().item():.4f}")

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()

        # # Check for gradient issues
        # if torch.rand(1).item() < 0.01:
        #     total_norm = 0
        #     for p in self.network.parameters():
        #         if p.grad is not None:
        #             param_norm = p.grad.data.norm(2)
        #             total_norm += param_norm.item() ** 2
        #     total_norm = total_norm ** (1. / 2)
        #     print(f"Gradient norm: {total_norm:.4f}")

        optimizer.step()

        # Update the EMA copy. This MUST run: `denoise(training=False)` - used by
        # generate(), test_step() and plot_images() - reads from `ema_network`, so if the
        # EMA is never updated, every sample and validation loss comes from an untrained net.
        with torch.no_grad():
            for ema_param, param in zip(self.ema_network.parameters(), self.network.parameters()):
                ema_param.copy_(self.ema_decay * ema_param + (1.0 - self.ema_decay) * param)
            # Buffers (e.g. BatchNorm running stats) are copied straight across.
            for ema_buf, buf in zip(self.ema_network.buffers(), self.network.buffers()):
                ema_buf.copy_(buf)

        return loss.item()

    def test_step(self, images, loss_fn):
        images = (images - self.normalizer_mean) / self.normalizer_std
        noises = torch.randn_like(images)

        diffusion_times = torch.rand((images.size(0), 1, 1, 1), device=images.device)
        noise_rates, signal_rates = self.schedule_fn(diffusion_times)
        noisy_images = signal_rates * images + noise_rates * noises

        with torch.no_grad():
            pred_noises, _ = self.denoise(noisy_images, noise_rates, signal_rates, training=False)
            loss = loss_fn(pred_noises, noises)

        return loss.item()

    def plot_images(self, epoch=None, logs=None, num_rows=3, num_cols=6):
        # plot random generated images for visual evaluation of generation quality
        generated_images = self.generate(
            num_images=num_rows * num_cols,
            image_size=IMAGE_SIZE,
            diffusion_steps=20,
        ).cpu()
        show_image(generated_images[0])
```

```python
from tqdm import tqdm
import os

def train_diffusion(model, train_loader, val_loader, optimizer, loss_fn, epochs=50, device='cuda', checkpoint_dir='checkpoints'):
    # Create checkpoint directory
    os.makedirs(checkpoint_dir, exist_ok=True)

    model.to(device)
    best_val_loss = float('inf')

    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        train_losses = []
        loader_with_progress = tqdm(train_loader, ncols=120, desc=f'Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs} [Train]')
        for images, _  in loader_with_progress:
            images = images.to(device)
            loss = model.train_step(images, optimizer, loss_fn)
            train_losses.append(loss)
            loader_with_progress.set_postfix(loss=f'{loss:.4f}')

        avg_train_loss = sum(train_losses) / len(train_losses)

        model.eval()
        model.plot_images()

        val_losses = []
        for images, _ in tqdm(val_loader, desc=f"Epoch {epoch+1} [Val]"):
            images = images.to(device)
            loss = model.test_step(images, loss_fn)
            val_losses.append(loss)

        avg_val_loss = sum(val_losses) / len(val_losses)
        loader_with_progress.set_postfix(loss=f'{avg_train_loss:.4f}')

        # Save checkpoint every epoch
        checkpoint = {
            'epoch': epoch + 1,
            'model_state_dict': model.network.state_dict(),
            'ema_model_state_dict': model.ema_network.state_dict(),
            'optimizer_state_dict': optimizer.state_dict(),
            'train_loss': avg_train_loss,
            'val_loss': avg_val_loss,
            'normalizer_mean': model.normalizer_mean,
            'normalizer_std': model.normalizer_std
        }

        # Save latest checkpoint
        checkpoint_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir, f'diffusion_epoch_{epoch+1:03d}.pth')
        torch.save(checkpoint, checkpoint_path)

        # Save best model
        if avg_val_loss < best_val_loss:
            best_val_loss = avg_val_loss
            best_checkpoint_path = os.path.join(checkpoint_dir, 'diffusion_best.pth')
            torch.save(checkpoint, best_checkpoint_path)
            print(f"New best model saved at epoch {epoch+1} with val_loss: {avg_val_loss:.4f}")

        print(f"Epoch {epoch+1} | Train Loss: {avg_train_loss:.4f} | Val Loss: {avg_val_loss:.4f}")
        print(f"Checkpoint saved: {checkpoint_path}")

def load_checkpoint(model, optimizer, checkpoint_path, device='cuda'):
    """
    Load a saved checkpoint and restore model, EMA, and optimizer states
    """
    checkpoint = torch.load(checkpoint_path, map_location=device)

    model.network.load_state_dict(checkpoint['model_state_dict'])
    model.ema_network.load_state_dict(checkpoint['ema_model_state_dict'])
    optimizer.load_state_dict(checkpoint['optimizer_state_dict'])

    # Restore normalizer settings
    model.normalizer_mean = checkpoint['normalizer_mean']
    model.normalizer_std = checkpoint['normalizer_std']

    print(f"Loaded checkpoint from epoch {checkpoint['epoch']}")
    print(f"Train Loss: {checkpoint['train_loss']:.4f}, Val Loss: {checkpoint['val_loss']:.4f}")

    return checkpoint['epoch']
```

```python
    mean.reshape(1, NUM_CHANNELS, 1, 1).to(device),
    std.reshape(1, NUM_CHANNELS, 1, 1).to(device),
)

train_diffusion(
    diffusion_model, train_loader, test_loader, optimizer, loss_fn,
    epochs=EPOCHS, device=device,
)
```

# Module 8 — Practical: Building a GPT from Scratch

In this practical you will build a **decoder-only Transformer** (a miniature GPT) in plain
PyTorch and train it to continue text in the style of *The Count of Monte Cristo*.

Everything is written out explicitly — no `transformers` library — so you can see exactly
how the pieces fit together.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this notebook you should be able to:

1. **Preprocess** a raw text corpus into a word-level vocabulary and an integer token stream.
2. Explain **why** a language model needs a *causal* (look-ahead) attention mask, and see one.
3. Describe what **token** and **positional** embeddings each contribute.
4. Assemble multi-head attention + feed-forward + layer-norm into a **Transformer block**.
5. Train the model with a **next-token prediction** objective and read a loss/perplexity curve.
6. **Visualise attention** and understand what the model is looking at.
7. Generate text and explain how **temperature** controls the randomness of sampling.

## Roadmap

| Section | What happens |
|---|---|
| 0 | Setup — imports, reproducibility, CPU/GPU selection |
| 1 | Load the corpus and look at the raw text |
| 2 | Clean, tokenize, and **visualise** the word distribution |
| 3 | Build the vocabulary and encode the corpus |
| 4 | Turn the token stream into (input, target) training pairs |
| 5 | The causal attention mask — with a picture |
| 6 | Token + positional embeddings |
| 7 | The Transformer block |
| 8 | Assemble the GPT and count parameters |
| 9 | Train, and plot the learning curve |
| 10 | Visualise what attention learned |
| 11 | Generate text; explore temperature |
| 12 | Summary + exercises |

> **Runtime.** On a GPU the default settings train in 1–2 minutes. On a laptop CPU budget
> roughly 4–8 minutes. Section 0 lets you dial this down if you are in a hurry.

## 0. Setup

We import the libraries, fix the random seeds so your run matches the text below, and pick
the compute device.

**About the device.** The notebook runs on all three backends:

| Backend | When it is picked | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `cuda` | NVIDIA GPU (Google Colab, workstation) | Fastest. |
| `mps` | Apple-silicon Mac (M1/M2/M3/M4) | Uses the built-in GPU. |
| `cpu` | Everything else | Always works, just slower. |

`DEVICE_OVERRIDE` below lets you force a specific backend — useful for debugging, since
CPU error messages are far more readable than GPU ones. Leave it as `None` for auto-detect.

```python
import re
import math
import time
from collections import Counter

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- reproducibility
SEED = 42
torch.manual_seed(SEED)
np.random.seed(SEED)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- device selection
# Set to "cpu", "cuda" or "mps" to force a backend; leave None to auto-detect.
DEVICE_OVERRIDE = None

def pick_device(override=None):
    """Return the best available torch.device, or the one the user asked for."""
    if override is not None:
        return torch.device(override)
    if torch.cuda.is_available():
        return torch.device("cuda")
    if torch.backends.mps.is_available():
        return torch.device("mps")
    return torch.device("cpu")

device = pick_device(DEVICE_OVERRIDE)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- training budget
# Number of optimiser steps. The default gives readable text in a few minutes.
# Drop to ~800 for a very quick smoke test, raise to ~8000 for noticeably better text.
TRAIN_STEPS = 2500 if device.type != "cpu" else 2000

print(f"PyTorch {torch.__version__}")
print(f"Using device: {device}")
if device.type == "cuda":
    print(f"  GPU: {torch.cuda.get_device_name(0)}")
    print(f"  Memory: {torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).total_memory / 1e9:.1f} GB")
elif device.type == "mps":
    print("  Apple-silicon GPU (Metal Performance Shaders)")
else:
    print("  No GPU detected - running on CPU (slower, but everything still works).")
print(f"Training budget: {TRAIN_STEPS} steps")
```

## 1. Load the corpus

A language model needs a lot of text. We use ***The Count of Monte Cristo*** by Alexandre
Dumas, downloaded straight from [Project Gutenberg](https://www.gutenberg.org/) (public
domain).

Gutenberg files wrap the actual book in a licence header and footer. If we left those in,
the model would happily learn to generate legal boilerplate — so the first job is to slice
out just the novel.

```python
import os
import urllib.request

GUTENBERG_URL = "https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/1184/pg1184.txt"
CACHE_PATH = "monte_cristo.txt"

# Cache locally so re-running the notebook does not hammer Project Gutenberg.
if os.path.exists(CACHE_PATH):
    with open(CACHE_PATH, "r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        raw_text = fh.read()
    print(f"Loaded cached copy from {CACHE_PATH}")
else:
    with urllib.request.urlopen(GUTENBERG_URL, timeout=60) as resp:
        raw_text = resp.read().decode("utf-8")
    with open(CACHE_PATH, "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        fh.write(raw_text)
    print(f"Downloaded and cached to {CACHE_PATH}")

print(f"Full file: {len(raw_text):,} characters")

# Keep only the novel itself: from the first chapter heading to the last one.
start_idx = raw_text.find("Chapter 1")
end_idx = raw_text.rfind("Chapter 5")
text = raw_text[start_idx:end_idx]

print(f"After stripping the Gutenberg header/footer: {len(text):,} characters")
print(f"  (dropped {len(raw_text) - len(text):,} characters of licence boilerplate)")
```

text:
## 2. Clean and tokenize

Neural networks consume numbers, not characters. Getting from one to the other takes two
steps: **tokenization** (split the text into units) and **encoding** (map units to integers).

We use the simplest scheme that works — **word-level** tokenization:

| Step | What we do | Why | What it costs us |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lowercase | `"The"` → `"the"` | Halves the vocabulary; `The`/`the` mean the same thing | Loses proper-noun and sentence-start cues |
| Strip punctuation | `re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9\s]", "", text)` | Avoids a separate token for every `,` `.` `"` | The model can never produce punctuation |
| Split on whitespace | `text.split()` | Trivial and fast | `"dont"` and `"don't"` collapse together |

> **Reality check.** Real GPT models use **subword** tokenization (BPE / SentencePiece),
> which keeps punctuation and casing and never produces an unknown token, because rare
> words get broken into familiar pieces. We use word-level here because you can *read* the
> tokens, which makes everything downstream easier to debug. The trade-off is a fixed
> vocabulary and an `<UNK>` token for anything outside it.

```python
sample_before = text[500:760]

# 1) drop every character that is not a letter, digit or whitespace
clean_text = re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9\s]", "", text)
# 2) case-fold
clean_text = clean_text.lower()
# 3) split on any run of whitespace
tokens = clean_text.split()

print("BEFORE cleaning:")
print(repr(sample_before))
print("\nAFTER cleaning:")
print(repr(re.sub(r"[^a-zA-Z0-9\s]", "", sample_before).lower()))

print("\n" + "=" * 70)
print(f"Total tokens (corpus length) : {len(tokens):,}")
print(f"Unique tokens (vocabulary)   : {len(set(tokens)):,}")
print(f"Type/token ratio             : {len(set(tokens)) / len(tokens):.4f}")
print(f"\nFirst 25 tokens: {tokens[:25]}")
```

text:
### 2.1 Visualising the corpus

Before modelling anything, look at your data. Four plots tell us almost everything we need
to know about this corpus:

1. **Top-20 words** — are the most common words the boring function words we expect?
2. **Zipf's law** — plotting frequency against rank on log-log axes should give a near
straight line. Natural language famously obeys this: the *n*-th most common word appears
roughly proportional to 1/*n*. This is *why* a small vocabulary can still cover most text.
3. **Cumulative coverage** — what fraction of the corpus do the top *k* words account for?
This is the plot that justifies our choice of vocabulary size in Section 3.
4. **Word-length distribution** — a sanity check that cleaning did not mangle the text.

**What to look for:** a steep Zipf line and a coverage curve that shoots up and then
flattens. The flattening point is the sweet spot for vocabulary size — past it you are
adding thousands of embedding parameters to cover a handful of extra words.

```python
counter = Counter(tokens)
freqs_sorted = np.array([c for _, c in counter.most_common()])
total_tokens = freqs_sorted.sum()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 9))

# --- (1) the 20 most frequent words -------------------------------------------
top20 = counter.most_common(20)
words, counts = zip(*top20)
axes[0, 0].barh(range(len(words))[::-1], counts, color="steelblue")
axes[0, 0].set_yticks(range(len(words))[::-1])
axes[0, 0].set_yticklabels(words)
axes[0, 0].set_xlabel("occurrences")
axes[0, 0].set_title("Top 20 most frequent words")

# --- (2) Zipf's law -----------------------------------------------------------
ranks = np.arange(1, len(freqs_sorted) + 1)
axes[0, 1].loglog(ranks, freqs_sorted, lw=1.6, color="darkorange", label="observed")
# ideal Zipf reference: f(r) = f(1) / r
axes[0, 1].loglog(ranks, freqs_sorted[0] / ranks, "k--", lw=1, label="ideal Zipf  f ∝ 1/rank")
axes[0, 1].set_xlabel("word rank (log)")
axes[0, 1].set_ylabel("frequency (log)")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Zipf's law: frequency vs rank")
axes[0, 1].legend()

# --- (3) cumulative coverage --------------------------------------------------
coverage = np.cumsum(freqs_sorted) / total_tokens
axes[1, 0].plot(ranks, coverage * 100, lw=2, color="seagreen")
for k in (1000, 5000, 9998):
    if k < len(coverage):
        pct = coverage[k - 1] * 100
        axes[1, 0].plot([k, k], [0, pct], ":", color="grey", lw=1)
        axes[1, 0].annotate(f"{k:,} words → {pct:.1f}%", xy=(k, pct),
                            xytext=(k * 1.05, pct - 9), fontsize=9)
axes[1, 0].set_xscale("log")
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("vocabulary size (log)")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("% of corpus covered")
axes[1, 0].set_title("Cumulative coverage vs vocabulary size")
axes[1, 0].set_ylim(0, 102)
axes[1, 0].grid(alpha=0.3)

# --- (4) word-length distribution ---------------------------------------------
lengths = [len(w) for w in tokens]
axes[1, 1].hist(lengths, bins=range(1, 20), color="indianred", edgecolor="white", align="left")
axes[1, 1].axvline(np.mean(lengths), color="k", ls="--",
                   label=f"mean = {np.mean(lengths):.2f} chars")
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel("word length (characters)")
axes[1, 1].set_ylabel("count")
axes[1, 1].set_title("Word-length distribution")
axes[1, 1].legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

hapax = sum(1 for c in counter.values() if c == 1)
print(f"Words appearing exactly once (hapax legomena): {hapax:,}"
      f"  ({hapax / len(counter):.1%} of the vocabulary, but only "
      f"{hapax / total_tokens:.2%} of all tokens)")
print("--> This is the key insight: most *distinct* words are rare, "
      "but most *token occurrences* come from a small set of common words.")
```

text:
## 3. Build the vocabulary and encode the corpus

The coverage plot above showed that a few thousand words already cover almost all of the
text. We cap the vocabulary at **10,000** entries:

- index `0` → `<PAD>` — padding, reserved (we do not actually need it here, but keeping
index 0 free for padding is near-universal convention).
- index `1` → `<UNK>` — the catch-all for any word outside the top 9,998.
- indices `2 … 9999` → the 9,998 most frequent words, **ordered by frequency**.

Ordering by frequency is a small but handy trick: low indices mean common words, so you can
eyeball an encoded sequence and immediately tell whether it is mostly common vocabulary.

We build two lookup tables:

- `vocab`: `word -> index`, used to **encode** text for the model.
- `inv_vocab`: `index -> word`, used to **decode** the model's output back to readable text.

```python
VOCAB_SIZE = 10_000

# 9,998 real words + <PAD> + <UNK> = VOCAB_SIZE
vocab = {word: idx + 2 for idx, (word, _) in enumerate(counter.most_common(VOCAB_SIZE - 2))}
vocab["<PAD>"] = 0
vocab["<UNK>"] = 1
inv_vocab = {idx: word for word, idx in vocab.items()}

# Encode the whole corpus: every token becomes an integer.
encoded = [vocab.get(word, vocab["<UNK>"]) for word in tokens]

n_unk = sum(1 for i in encoded if i == 1)
print(f"Vocabulary size : {len(vocab):,}")
print(f"Encoded corpus  : {len(encoded):,} token ids")
print(f"<UNK> rate      : {n_unk / len(encoded):.2%}  "
      f"(= how often the model sees a word it cannot name)")

print("\nSample of the mapping (word -> id):")
for word in ["the", "count", "monte", "cristo", "dantes", "zzzznotaword"]:
    idx = vocab.get(word, 1)
    tag = "" if word in vocab else "   <- not in vocab, falls back to <UNK>"
    print(f"  {word:>14s} -> {idx:5d}{tag}")

print("\nRound-trip check (encode then decode the first 15 tokens):")
print("  original :", " ".join(tokens[:15]))
print("  ids      :", encoded[:15])
print("  decoded  :", " ".join(inv_vocab[i] for i in encoded[:15]))
```

text:
## 4. From a token stream to training pairs

A GPT is trained on one deceptively simple task: **given the tokens so far, predict the
next one**. We never need labels — the text *is* the label.

We slide a window of `SEQ_LEN = 30` tokens over the corpus. For each window:

- **input** = `tokens[i : i+30]`
- **target** = `tokens[i+1 : i+31]` ← the same window, shifted one step left

```
index: 0 1 2 3 4 ...
input (x): the count of monte cristo ...
target (y): count of monte cristo had ...
^ ^ ^ ^ ^
| | | | |
predict the next word at EVERY position, not just the last one
```

That last point matters. One window of 30 tokens gives us **30 separate prediction
problems**, all solved in a single forward pass. This is what makes Transformer training so
efficient compared with an RNN — and it is *only* possible because the causal mask
(Section 5) stops position *k* from peeking at position *k+1*.

```python
SEQ_LEN = 30
BATCH_SIZE = 64


class TextDataset(Dataset):
    """Sliding windows over a flat list of token ids.

    Item i is the pair (tokens[i : i+SEQ_LEN], tokens[i+1 : i+SEQ_LEN+1]).
    """

    def __init__(self, data):
        self.data = data

    def __len__(self):
        # -SEQ_LEN so the shifted target never runs off the end of the list
        return len(self.data) - SEQ_LEN

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        return (
            torch.tensor(self.data[idx : idx + SEQ_LEN], dtype=torch.long),
            torch.tensor(self.data[idx + 1 : idx + SEQ_LEN + 1], dtype=torch.long),
        )


# Hold out the last 5% of the corpus so we can tell memorisation from generalisation.
split = int(0.95 * len(encoded))
train_dataset = TextDataset(encoded[:split])
val_dataset = TextDataset(encoded[split:])

# Worker processes + pinned memory pay off on CUDA; on CPU/MPS they usually cost more
# than they save for a dataset this small.
NUM_WORKERS = 2 if device.type == "cuda" else 0
PIN_MEMORY = device.type == "cuda"

train_loader = DataLoader(
    train_dataset, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=True, drop_last=True,
    num_workers=NUM_WORKERS, pin_memory=PIN_MEMORY,
)
val_loader = DataLoader(
    val_dataset, batch_size=BATCH_SIZE, shuffle=False, drop_last=True,
    num_workers=NUM_WORKERS, pin_memory=PIN_MEMORY,
)

print(f"Training windows   : {len(train_dataset):,}  ({len(train_loader):,} batches/epoch)")
print(f"Validation windows : {len(val_dataset):,}  ({len(val_loader):,} batches)")
```

Let's decode one real training pair back into words and confirm the target really is the
input shifted by one. **This is the single most valuable debugging check in any language
modelling pipeline** — an off-by-one here silently destroys training.

```python
example_inputs, example_targets = next(iter(train_loader))

print(f"inputs  shape: {tuple(example_inputs.shape)}   (batch, sequence)")
print(f"targets shape: {tuple(example_targets.shape)}")
print(f"dtype: {example_inputs.dtype}\n")

x0, y0 = example_inputs[0], example_targets[0]
print(f"{'pos':>4}  {'input id':>9}  {'input word':<16}  {'target id':>9}  {'target word':<16}")
print("-" * 68)
for pos in range(10):
    print(f"{pos:>4}  {x0[pos].item():>9}  {inv_vocab[x0[pos].item()]:<16}"
          f"  {y0[pos].item():>9}  {inv_vocab[y0[pos].item()]:<16}")
print("   ...")

print("\ninput  text:", " ".join(inv_vocab[i.item()] for i in x0))
print("target text:", " ".join(inv_vocab[i.item()] for i in y0))

shifted_ok = torch.equal(x0[1:], y0[:-1])
print(f"\nTarget == input shifted left by one?  {shifted_ok}")
assert shifted_ok, "Off-by-one in the dataset! Training would not work."
```

text:
## 5. The causal (look-ahead) mask

Self-attention, left alone, lets **every** position see **every** other position. For
translation or classification that is exactly what you want. For a language model it is a
catastrophe: position 5 would be allowed to look at position 6 — the very word it is
supposed to predict. The model would learn to copy the answer and score a perfect training
loss while being completely useless at generation.

The fix is a **causal mask**: position *i* may attend to position *j* only when `j <= i`.

$$
\text{mask}[i, j] = \begin{cases} 1 & j \le i \quad \text{(allowed — past and present)} \\
0 & j > i \quad \text{(blocked — the future)} \end{cases}
$$

This gives a lower-triangular matrix of ones. In practice the blocked entries have their
attention *scores* set to $-\infty$ **before** the softmax, so after softmax their weight is
exactly 0.

> **Watch the convention.** PyTorch's `nn.MultiheadAttention` takes a boolean `attn_mask`
> where **`True` means "block this position"** — the opposite of the matrix above. That is
> why you will see `attn_mask=~causal_mask` in the code: we build the intuitive
> "allowed" matrix, then invert it at the call site. Getting this backwards is one of the
> most common Transformer bugs.

```python
# The mask is built with a broadcasting trick. Two 1-D ranges, reshaped into a
# column and a row, compare elementwise into a full 2-D matrix:
i = torch.arange(5).unsqueeze(1)   # shape (5, 1) - the "destination" / query position
j = torch.arange(5).unsqueeze(0)   # shape (1, 5) - the "source" / key position

print("i (queries, column vector):\n", i)
print("\nj (keys, row vector):\n", j)
print("\ni >= j  broadcasts to a (5, 5) lower-triangular matrix:\n", (i >= j).int())
```

```python
def causal_attention_mask(n_dest, n_src, device):
    """True where attention is ALLOWED (query i may look at key j iff j <= i)."""
    i = torch.arange(n_dest, device=device).unsqueeze(1)
    j = torch.arange(n_src, device=device).unsqueeze(0)
    return i >= j


demo_mask = causal_attention_mask(8, 8, device)
print("Causal mask for a length-8 sequence (1 = may attend, 0 = blocked):\n")
print("       " + "".join(f"k{j} " for j in range(8)))
for q in range(8):
    row = "".join(f" {v}  " for v in demo_mask[q].int().tolist())
    print(f"  q{q}  {row}  <- position {q} may look at {q + 1} of 8 positions")

print(f"\nAllowed pairs: {demo_mask.sum().item()} of {demo_mask.numel()} "
      f"({demo_mask.float().mean().item():.0%}) - a causal model does roughly "
      "half the attention work of a bidirectional one.")
```

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4.6))

# --- (1) the mask itself, at the real sequence length -------------------------
full_mask = causal_attention_mask(SEQ_LEN, SEQ_LEN, torch.device("cpu")).int().numpy()
im0 = axes[0].imshow(full_mask, cmap="Greys_r", interpolation="nearest")
axes[0].set_title(f"Causal mask ({SEQ_LEN}x{SEQ_LEN})\nwhite = allowed, black = blocked")
axes[0].set_xlabel("key position j  (attending TO)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("query position i  (attending FROM)")
plt.colorbar(im0, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046)

# --- (2) random attention scores BEFORE masking -------------------------------
torch.manual_seed(0)
scores = torch.randn(SEQ_LEN, SEQ_LEN)
unmasked = torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1).numpy()
im1 = axes[1].imshow(unmasked, cmap="viridis", interpolation="nearest")
axes[1].set_title("Attention WITHOUT the mask\n(every position sees the future)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("key position j")
axes[1].set_ylabel("query position i")
plt.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.046)

# --- (3) the same scores AFTER masking ----------------------------------------
allowed = causal_attention_mask(SEQ_LEN, SEQ_LEN, torch.device("cpu"))
masked_scores = scores.masked_fill(~allowed, float("-inf"))
masked = torch.softmax(masked_scores, dim=-1).numpy()
im2 = axes[2].imshow(masked, cmap="viridis", interpolation="nearest")
axes[2].set_title("Attention WITH the mask\n(strictly lower-triangular)")
axes[2].set_xlabel("key position j")
```

text:
## 6. Token and positional embeddings

Attention is **permutation-equivariant**: shuffle the input tokens and the output shuffles
with them, otherwise unchanged. On its own it has no idea that *"the dog bit the man"*
differs from *"the man bit the dog"*. We have to inject word order explicitly.

So each input token gets **two** vectors, which are simply added together:

| Embedding | Lookup table | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| **Token** | `nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)` | *what* is this word? |
| **Position** | `nn.Embedding(max_len, embed_dim)` | *where* in the sequence is it? |

$$\text{input}_k = E_{\text{token}}[x_k] + E_{\text{pos}}[k]$$

Adding (rather than concatenating) keeps the dimensionality constant and works well in
practice — the network has plenty of capacity to disentangle the two signals.

We use **learned** positional embeddings, as GPT-2 does: the position vectors are ordinary
parameters trained by backprop. The original *Attention Is All You Need* paper instead used
fixed sinusoids. In Section 10 we will plot what our learned positions actually look like.

```python
class TokenAndPositionEmbedding(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, max_len, vocab_size, embed_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.token_emb = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim)
        self.pos_emb = nn.Embedding(max_len, embed_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        positions = torch.arange(x.size(1), device=x.device).unsqueeze(0)
        pos_embeddings = self.pos_emb(positions)
        token_embeddings = self.token_emb(x)
        return token_embeddings + pos_embeddings
```

text:
## 7. The Transformer block

One block is two sub-layers, each wrapped in a residual connection and a layer norm:

```
x ──┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ │
▼ │
masked multi-head attention │ tokens exchange information
│ │
▼ │
dropout │
│ ▼
(+) ◄──────────────────────────── residual
│
LayerNorm
│
├──────────────────────────────┐
▼ │
feed-forward (d -> ff -> d) │ each token processed independently
│ │
▼ ▼
(+) ◄──────────────────────────── residual
│
LayerNorm
│
▼
```

The division of labour is the thing to remember:

- **Attention mixes across positions.** It is the only place where tokens talk to each
other.
- **The feed-forward network mixes across features.** It sees one position at a time and
does the per-token "thinking". It is also where most of the parameters live.
- **Residual connections** give gradients a clean path back to the embeddings, which is
what makes deep stacks trainable at all.
- **Multi-head** means attention is split into `num_heads` parallel sub-spaces, each free
to track a different relationship (one head might follow syntax, another coreference).

Note this block applies LayerNorm *after* the residual add ("post-norm", as in the original
paper). Modern LLMs usually use "pre-norm", which is more stable for very deep stacks. With
a single block it makes no practical difference.

```python
class TransformerBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, num_heads, embed_dim, ff_dim, dropout_rate=0.1):
        super().__init__()
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(
            embed_dim, num_heads, dropout=dropout_rate, batch_first=True
        )
        self.ln_1 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)
        self.dropout_1 = nn.Dropout(dropout_rate)

        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(embed_dim, ff_dim),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(ff_dim, embed_dim),
            nn.Dropout(dropout_rate),
        )
        self.ln_2 = nn.LayerNorm(embed_dim)

    def forward(self, x):
        seq_len = x.size(1)

        # `allowed[i, j]` is True when query i may attend to key j.
        allowed = causal_attention_mask(seq_len, seq_len, x.device)
        # nn.MultiheadAttention wants the OPPOSITE polarity: True == "block this".
        attn_output, attn_weights = self.attn(
            x, x, x,
            attn_mask=~allowed,
            need_weights=True,
            average_attn_weights=True,   # average over heads -> (batch, seq, seq)
        )

        # sub-layer 1: attention + residual + norm
        x = self.ln_1(x + self.dropout_1(attn_output))
        # sub-layer 2: feed-forward + residual + norm
        x = self.ln_2(x + self.ffn(x))
        return x, attn_weights
```

text:
## 8. Assemble the GPT

The full model is just three stages:

```
token ids (batch, 30)
│
▼
TokenAndPositionEmbedding (batch, 30, embed_dim)
│
▼
TransformerBlock (batch, 30, embed_dim)
│
▼
Linear "language-model head" (batch, 30, vocab_size) <- one score per vocabulary word,
at every position
```

Our configuration:

| Hyperparameter | Value | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `embed_dim` | 256 | Width of every vector in the model |
| `num_heads` | 8 | 256 / 8 = 32 dimensions per head |
| `ff_dim` | 512 | Feed-forward hidden width (2× `embed_dim`) |
| blocks | 1 | Real GPT-2 has 12–48; one is enough to see the idea |
| `SEQ_LEN` | 30 | Context window |

A real GPT stacks many blocks. We use one so that training finishes in minutes and so the
attention map in Section 10 is directly interpretable — with 12 stacked blocks, attention
weights become very hard to read.

```python
class GPT(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, max_len, vocab_size, embed_dim, num_heads, ff_dim):
        super().__init__()
        self.embed = TokenAndPositionEmbedding(max_len, vocab_size, embed_dim)
        self.transformer = TransformerBlock(num_heads, embed_dim, ff_dim)
        self.lm_head = nn.Linear(embed_dim, vocab_size)

    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.embed(x)                     # (B, L) -> (B, L, D)
        x, attn_weights = self.transformer(x) # (B, L, D)
        logits = self.lm_head(x)              # (B, L, vocab_size)
        return logits, attn_weights
```

```python
EMBED_DIM = 256
NUM_HEADS = 8
FF_DIM = 512

model = GPT(SEQ_LEN, VOCAB_SIZE, EMBED_DIM, NUM_HEADS, FF_DIM).to(device)

# --- where do the parameters actually live? -----------------------------------
groups = {
    "token embedding":    model.embed.token_emb,
    "position embedding": model.embed.pos_emb,
    "attention":          model.transformer.attn,
    "feed-forward":       model.transformer.ffn,
    "layer norms":        nn.ModuleList([model.transformer.ln_1, model.transformer.ln_2]),
    "lm head":            model.lm_head,
}
total = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

print(f"{'component':<22} {'parameters':>12}   share")

for name, module in groups.items():

    print(f"{name:<22} {n:>12,}   {n / total:>5.1%}")

print(f"{'TOTAL':<22} {total:>12,}")

print("Note how much of a small LM is just the embedding + output table - that is the "
      "cost of a 10,000-word vocabulary.")

    probe_logits, probe_attn = model(example_inputs[:2].to(device))
```

text:
## 9. Training

The objective is plain **cross-entropy** over the vocabulary, applied at every position:

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k} \log P(x_{k+1} \mid x_{\le k})$$

To feed `nn.CrossEntropyLoss` we flatten the batch and sequence axes together:

- logits `(B, L, V)` → `(B·L, V)`
- targets `(B, L)` → `(B·L,)`

so a batch of 64 windows of 30 tokens becomes 1,920 independent classification problems.

**Perplexity** is the number we actually report, because it has a meaning:

$$\text{PPL} = e^{\mathcal{L}}$$

It is roughly *"how many words is the model effectively choosing between at each step"*.
Random guessing over our 10,000-word vocabulary gives PPL = 10,000. Anything well below
that means the model has learned something real.

We also evaluate on the held-out 5% every so often, so you can watch for the train and
validation curves separating — the signature of overfitting.

```python
from tqdm.auto import tqdm


@torch.no_grad()
def evaluate(model, loader, criterion, device, max_batches=40):
    """Average cross-entropy on a held-out loader."""
    model.eval()
    total, n = 0.0, 0
    for i, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(loader):
        if i >= max_batches:
            break
        logits, _ = model(inputs.to(device))
        loss = criterion(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.to(device).reshape(-1))
        total += loss.item()
        n += 1
    model.train()
    return total / max(n, 1)


def train_gpt(model, train_loader, val_loader, optimizer, criterion, device,
              total_steps, eval_every=250):
    """Train for `total_steps` optimiser steps, recording history for plotting."""
    model.to(device)
    model.train()

    history = {"step": [], "train_loss": [], "val_step": [], "val_loss": []}
    running, step = [], 0
    start = time.time()

    pbar = tqdm(total=total_steps, ncols=110, desc="training")
    while step < total_steps:
        for inputs, targets in train_loader:
            inputs = inputs.to(device, non_blocking=PIN_MEMORY)
            targets = targets.to(device, non_blocking=PIN_MEMORY)

            optimizer.zero_grad()
            logits, _ = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(logits.reshape(-1, logits.size(-1)), targets.reshape(-1))
            loss.backward()
            # Clipping keeps a rare bad batch from blowing up the run.
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
            optimizer.step()

            running.append(loss.item())
            step += 1
            pbar.update(1)

            if step % 25 == 0:
                avg = float(np.mean(running[-25:]))
                history["step"].append(step)
                history["train_loss"].append(avg)
                pbar.set_postfix({"loss": f"{avg:.3f}", "ppl": f"{math.exp(avg):7.1f}"})

            if step % eval_every == 0 or step == total_steps:
                vl = evaluate(model, val_loader, criterion, device)
                history["val_step"].append(step)
                history["val_loss"].append(vl)

            if step >= total_steps:
                break
    pbar.close()

    print(f"Finished {step} steps in {time.time() - start:.0f}s on {device}")
    return history
```

```python
LEARNING_RATE = 3e-4

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=LEARNING_RATE)
# ignore_index=0 means <PAD> positions never contribute to the loss.
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=0)

print(f"Training for {TRAIN_STEPS} steps on {device} "
      f"(batch {BATCH_SIZE} x seq {SEQ_LEN} = {BATCH_SIZE * SEQ_LEN:,} predictions/step)")
print(f"Random-guess baseline: loss = ln({VOCAB_SIZE:,}) = {math.log(VOCAB_SIZE):.2f}, "
      f"perplexity = {VOCAB_SIZE:,}\n")

history = train_gpt(
    model, train_loader, val_loader, optimizer, criterion, device,
    total_steps=TRAIN_STEPS, eval_every=250,
)

final_train = history["train_loss"][-1]
final_val = history["val_loss"][-1]
print(f"\nFinal train loss {final_train:.3f}  (perplexity {math.exp(final_train):.1f})")
print(f"Final   val loss {final_val:.3f}  (perplexity {math.exp(final_val):.1f})")
print(f"Perplexity improved {VOCAB_SIZE / math.exp(final_val):.0f}x over random guessing.")
```

### 9.1 The learning curve

**How to read these plots:**

- *Left* — cross-entropy loss. Should fall steeply at first, then flatten. The dashed line
is the random-guessing baseline, `ln(10000) ≈ 9.21`.
- *Right* — the same thing as perplexity on a log scale, which is usually easier to
interpret. Watch it drop from 10,000 towards the low hundreds.

**The diagnostic that matters:** compare the train and validation curves.

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Both still falling | Under-trained — raise `TRAIN_STEPS` |
| Both flat and close | Converged for this model size |
| Train falling, validation rising | **Overfitting** — the model is memorising Dumas |

With only 2,000–2,500 steps over ~240,000 tokens we see less than one full pass through the
data, so overfitting is unlikely here. Push `TRAIN_STEPS` to 20,000 and the gap will open.


text:
## 10. Looking inside the model

A trained Transformer is not a black box — we can read its attention weights directly.

### 10.1 Attention heatmap

Row *i* of the heatmap is the probability distribution that position *i* spread over all
the positions it was allowed to see. Each row sums to 1.

**What to look for:**

- The upper-right triangle must be **exactly zero**. That is the causal mask doing its job.
If you see any colour up there, something is broken.
- A bright **diagonal / near-diagonal band** means the model relies heavily on the last few
words — unsurprising, since local context predicts the next word well.
- Bright **vertical stripes** mean one particular token is important to everyone — usually
a very frequent word like *"the"* that acts as an attention sink.
- The **first row** is always a single bright square: position 0 can only attend to itself.

```python
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    sample_x, _ = next(iter(val_loader))
    sample_x = sample_x[:1].to(device)
    _, attn = model(sample_x)

attn_map = attn[0].cpu().numpy()                       # (seq_len, seq_len)
words = [inv_vocab[i.item()] for i in sample_x[0].cpu()]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 6.5))

# --- full attention map with word labels --------------------------------------
im = axes[0].imshow(attn_map, cmap="viridis", interpolation="nearest")
axes[0].set_xticks(range(len(words)))
axes[0].set_xticklabels(words, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_yticks(range(len(words)))
axes[0].set_yticklabels(words, fontsize=8)
axes[0].set_xlabel("attending TO (key)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("attending FROM (query)")
axes[0].set_title("Learned attention (averaged over the 8 heads)")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046)

# --- how far back does attention reach? ---------------------------------------
# For each query position, the average weight placed at distance d back.
max_d = len(words)
dist_weight = np.zeros(max_d)
dist_count = np.zeros(max_d)
for q in range(max_d):
    for k in range(q + 1):
        dist_weight[q - k] += attn_map[q, k]
        dist_count[q - k] += 1
mean_by_distance = dist_weight / np.maximum(dist_count, 1)

axes[1].bar(range(max_d), mean_by_distance, color="darkorange")
axes[1].set_xlabel("distance back from the current token (0 = itself)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("mean attention weight")
axes[1].set_title("How far back does attention actually look?")
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

upper = np.triu(attn_map, k=1)
print(f"Max weight anywhere in the FUTURE (upper triangle): {upper.max():.2e}")
print("  -> effectively zero, so the causal mask is working.\n")
print(f"Row sums (should all be 1.0): min {attn_map.sum(1).min():.4f}, "
      f"max {attn_map.sum(1).max():.4f}")
print(f"\nMost-attended token overall: '{words[int(attn_map.sum(0).argmax())]}' "
      f"(position {int(attn_map.sum(0).argmax())})")
```

### 10.2 What did the embeddings learn?

Two more views into the trained model:

**Left — positional embedding similarity.** We take the 30 learned position vectors and
compute the cosine similarity of every pair. If the model learned anything about order, we
expect a bright diagonal with similarity *decaying smoothly* away from it: position 7 should
resemble positions 6 and 8 more than position 25. That smooth decay is the model discovering
the concept of "nearby" entirely from data — nobody told it that positions are ordered.

**Right — token embedding neighbourhoods.** For a few query words we list their nearest
neighbours in embedding space by cosine similarity. After only a couple of thousand steps
the neighbourhoods are noisy, but you should still see words of the same *grammatical
class* clustering (pronouns with pronouns, names with names).

```python
with torch.no_grad():
    pos_emb = model.embed.pos_emb.weight.detach().cpu()     # (SEQ_LEN, EMBED_DIM)
    tok_emb = model.embed.token_emb.weight.detach().cpu()   # (VOCAB_SIZE, EMBED_DIM)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.5))

# --- positional embedding similarity ------------------------------------------
pos_norm = F.normalize(pos_emb, dim=1)
pos_sim = (pos_norm @ pos_norm.T).numpy()
im = axes[0].imshow(pos_sim, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("position")
axes[0].set_ylabel("position")
axes[0].set_title("Cosine similarity between learned position embeddings")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.046)

# --- similarity as a function of distance -------------------------------------
offsets = range(SEQ_LEN)
mean_sim = [np.mean([pos_sim[i, i + d] for i in range(SEQ_LEN - d)]) for d in offsets]
axes[1].plot(list(offsets), mean_sim, "o-", color="seagreen", lw=2)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8, ls=":")
axes[1].set_xlabel("distance between two positions")
axes[1].set_ylabel("mean cosine similarity")
axes[1].set_title("Nearby positions should be more similar than distant ones")
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"similarity at distance 1 : {mean_sim[1]:+.3f}")
print(f"similarity at distance {SEQ_LEN-1}: {mean_sim[-1]:+.3f}")
print("  A downward trend means the model learned that position is ordered.\n")

# --- nearest neighbours in token-embedding space ------------------------------
tok_norm = F.normalize(tok_emb, dim=1)
print("Nearest neighbours in token-embedding space (cosine similarity):\n")
for query in ["he", "she", "count", "ship", "sea", "money"]:
    if query not in vocab:
        continue
    qi = vocab[query]
    sims = (tok_norm @ tok_norm[qi]).numpy()
    sims[qi] = -2.0                     # exclude the word itself
    sims[0] = sims[1] = -2.0            # exclude <PAD> / <UNK>
    top = np.argsort(sims)[-6:][::-1]
    neigh = ", ".join(f"{inv_vocab[int(i)]} ({sims[int(i)]:.2f})" for i in top)
    print(f"  {query:>8s} -> {neigh}")
```

text:
## 11. Generating text

Generation is a loop:

1. Encode the prompt into token ids.
2. Run a forward pass; keep only the logits at the **last** position.
3. Turn those logits into a probability distribution and **sample** one token.
4. Append it to the sequence and go back to step 2.

This is what *autoregressive* means — each new token becomes part of the input for the next.

### Temperature

Before the softmax we divide the logits by a **temperature** $T$:

$$P(w) = \frac{\exp(z_w / T)}{\sum_v \exp(z_v / T)}$$

| $T$ | Effect | Typical output |
|---|---|---|
| → 0 | Distribution collapses onto the argmax | Repetitive, often loops forever |
| 0.5 | Sharpened | Safe, fluent, a bit dull |
| 1.0 | The model's true distribution | Balanced |
| 1.5+ | Flattened | Creative, then incoherent |

Two implementation details worth noting in the code below:

- We mask `<UNK>` by setting its logit to **`-inf`** (not to 0!). Setting a logit to zero
makes it *averagely likely*; only `-inf` makes it impossible after softmax.
- The context is truncated to the last `SEQ_LEN` tokens, because the positional embedding
table only has `SEQ_LEN` rows. Feeding more would raise an index error.

```python
class TextGenerator:
    def __init__(self, model, vocab, inv_vocab, device, seq_len):
        self.model = model.to(device)
        self.vocab = vocab
        self.inv_vocab = inv_vocab
        self.device = device
        self.seq_len = seq_len

    def _next_token_probs(self, logits, temperature, top_k=None):
        """Turn raw logits into a sampling distribution."""
        logits = logits.clone()

        # Never generate the special tokens. -inf (not 0!) is what makes a
        # token impossible: softmax(-inf) == 0, whereas softmax(0) is "average".
        logits[self.vocab["<PAD>"]] = float("-inf")
        logits[self.vocab["<UNK>"]] = float("-inf")

        logits = logits / max(temperature, 1e-6)

        if top_k is not None:
            kth = torch.topk(logits, top_k).values[-1]
            logits[logits < kth] = float("-inf")

        return F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    @torch.no_grad()
    def generate(self, prompt, max_new_tokens=60, temperature=1.0, top_k=None, verbose=True):
        self.model.eval()
        tokens = [self.vocab.get(w, self.vocab["<UNK>"]) for w in prompt.lower().split()]
        if not tokens:
            raise ValueError("Prompt produced no tokens.")

        steps = []
        for _ in range(max_new_tokens):
            # Only the last seq_len tokens fit in the positional embedding table.
            context = tokens[-self.seq_len:]
            x = torch.tensor([context], dtype=torch.long, device=self.device)

            logits, attn = self.model(x)
            probs = self._next_token_probs(logits[0, -1], temperature, top_k)
            next_id = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1).item()

            steps.append({"probs": probs.cpu(), "chosen": next_id,
                          "attn": attn[0].cpu()})
            tokens.append(next_id)

        words = [self.inv_vocab[i] for i in tokens]
        generated = " ".join(words)
        if verbose:
            print(f"[T={temperature}" + (f", top_k={top_k}" if top_k else "") + "]")
            print(generated)
            print()
        return generated, steps


generator = TextGenerator(model, vocab, inv_vocab, device, SEQ_LEN)
print("Generator ready.")
```

### 11.1 Seeing what temperature does

Rather than just reading the output, let's plot the actual next-token distribution the
model produces for one fixed prompt, under several temperatures.

- *Left* — the top-15 candidate words and their probabilities at each temperature. Low
temperature concentrates almost all the mass on one or two words; high temperature
spreads it out.
- *Right* — **entropy** of the full distribution, a single number summarising the same
thing. Entropy is measured in bits: 0 bits means "completely certain", and
$\log_2(10000) \approx 13.3$ bits would mean "no idea at all".

```python
probe_prompt = "the count of monte"
probe_ids = [vocab.get(w, 1) for w in probe_prompt.split()]

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    probe_logits, _ = model(torch.tensor([probe_ids], device=device))
    base_logits = probe_logits[0, -1].cpu()

TEMPS = [0.3, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5]
TOP_N = 15

# Rank candidates by the T=1.0 distribution so all four bars share an x-axis.
ranked = torch.topk(base_logits, TOP_N).indices
labels = [inv_vocab[int(i)] for i in ranked]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 5))

width = 0.2
xs = np.arange(TOP_N)
for k, temp in enumerate(TEMPS):
    lg = base_logits.clone()
    lg[0] = lg[1] = float("-inf")               # mask <PAD>/<UNK>
    p = F.softmax(lg / temp, dim=-1)
    axes[0].bar(xs + (k - 1.5) * width, p[ranked].numpy(), width,
                label=f"T = {temp}")

axes[0].set_xticks(xs)
axes[0].set_xticklabels(labels, rotation=60, ha="right")
axes[0].set_ylabel("probability")
axes[0].set_title(f"Next-token distribution after '{probe_prompt}'")
axes[0].legend()
axes[0].grid(alpha=0.3, axis="y")

# --- entropy across a fine temperature sweep ----------------------------------
sweep = np.linspace(0.1, 2.5, 60)
entropies, top1 = [], []
for temp in sweep:
    lg = base_logits.clone()
    lg[0] = lg[1] = float("-inf")
    p = F.softmax(lg / float(temp), dim=-1)
    p = p[p > 0]
    entropies.append(float(-(p * torch.log2(p)).sum()))
    top1.append(float(F.softmax(base_logits / float(temp), dim=-1).max()))

ax2 = axes[1]
ax2.plot(sweep, entropies, lw=2.2, color="purple", label="entropy (bits)")
ax2.axhline(math.log2(VOCAB_SIZE), ls="--", color="grey",
            label=f"uniform = {math.log2(VOCAB_SIZE):.1f} bits")
ax2.set_xlabel("temperature")
ax2.set_ylabel("entropy (bits)", color="purple")
ax2.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="purple")
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)

ax3 = ax2.twinx()
ax3.plot(sweep, top1, lw=2.2, color="darkorange", label="P(most likely token)")
ax3.set_ylabel("probability of the single best token", color="darkorange")
ax3.tick_params(axis="y", labelcolor="darkorange")

ax2.set_title("Low T -> confident and repetitive.  High T -> uncertain and creative.")
lines = ax2.get_lines() + ax3.get_lines()
ax2.legend(lines, [l.get_label() for l in lines], loc="center right")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

for temp in TEMPS:
    lg = base_logits.clone()
    lg[0] = lg[1] = float("-inf")
    p = F.softmax(lg / temp, dim=-1)
    pp = p[p > 0]
    ent = float(-(pp * torch.log2(pp)).sum())
    print(f"T = {temp:<4} entropy {ent:5.2f} bits | top word "
          f"'{inv_vocab[int(p.argmax())]}' at {p.max():.1%}")
```
